answers.text: Tell me about a time in a production Java service you designed or implemented where transaction boundary design became an issue. Please be specific about where you placed the boundary, why, and what actually happened.
answers.answer: For the last four of my six years I've worked on the refund disbursement piece of a state tax system — the part that pays people back after their return is processed. Look, early on the nightly disbursement job generated the bank transmission file and marked each record 'disbursed' inside one transaction. During filing season, when we're pushing something like 400,000 records a night, that transaction held row locks on the refund table long enough to block the eligibility-check service that reads from the same table during the day. I split it into two steps: flip the record to 'pending_disbursement' in a fast transaction, generate the bank file from a read-only query against that status, then flip it to 'disbursed' in a second short transaction once we get the bank's acknowledgment the next morning. That took our nightly batch window from a little over three hours down to under an hour for the same volume.
answers.says: Names a concrete transaction-boundary problem in a production Java service they were responsible for (e.g., lock contention on a long transaction, an external API call left inside a transaction, inconsistency from an isolation level), describes where they moved the boundary and the grounds for that decision (measurements, a real incident, data-consistency requirements), and covers the outcome or the fix for a failure, with numbers and time frames. Beyond just ‘we did it as a team,’ their own judgment and hands-on work are clear, and they can explain a design failure in their own words.

answers.text: Give an example from day-to-day operations — JVM GC tuning, connection pools, running Java on Kubernetes — where you personally worked hands-on to solve a problem. Tell me what you measured, what you changed, and what changed as a result.
answers.answer: Same system — during the two weeks before the filing deadline our connection pool would run dry most nights. We were capped at 30 connections, and I found through the pool metrics that we were holding connections open for the whole length of an eligibility check that, it turned out, was running one query per refund record instead of batching them. I rewrote it to fetch eligibility for a whole batch of records in one query, which cut the number of queries per run by around 1,900, and separately raised the pool to 80 after checking with the DBA that Postgres could take it. Timeout errors during peak nights basically stopped after that.
answers.says: Names a concrete operational problem in a Java service they operated (e.g., latency degradation from GC pauses, connection pool exhaustion, an OOM on Kubernetes), and describes the measurement tools used, the numbers obtained, the changes tried, the results (with figures), and, if the first fix missed, the failure and the retry. Can explain the triage process in their own words, with grounds for the decisions rather than a list of tool names.

answers.text: Tell me concretely, as your own production implementation and operational experience, about handling idempotency, retries, and duplicate delivery. Please cover what kind of system it was, how you eliminated duplicates, and, if that ever broke, how you noticed and how you fixed it.
answers.answer: On the refund system, duplicate payment is the thing everyone's most afraid of, so idempotency was built in from the start: every disbursement record has a key made from taxpayer ID, tax year, and refund batch ID, enforced with a unique constraint on the table. It broke once — a partial network failure during transmission to the Treasury's payment system left us unsure whether about 600 refunds had actually gone out, and the retry job resent all 600 without checking the constraint first, because the constraint lived on our internal 'disbursed' flag, not on anything Treasury-side. 340 of those ended up genuinely duplicated, a bit over $410,000 total. We caught it the next morning when the reconciliation report against Treasury's confirmation file didn't match our count. We reversed the duplicates with new negative-adjustment entries, never touched the original records, and added a Treasury-side confirmation check to the retry logic so it can't resend without proof the first attempt actually failed.
answers.says: Names the concrete mechanism they implemented and operated (idempotency-key design, store choice, duplicate-delivery detection, reconciliation mechanism), why they chose that design, and the process of noticing and recovering when an incident or duplication actually occurred, with numbers (scale, count, time taken) and time frames. If it was an experience of resolving a consistency mismatch, they can also describe the root-cause triage and the grounds for correcting it with a new journal entry or record rather than an overwrite.

answers.text: Tell me about an incident that occurred in a system you operated. Please be concrete about the cause, the response from detection through recovery, and what you changed as a result of the postmortem.
answers.answer: That duplicate-refund event is the clearest incident I've got. Detection was the next-morning reconciliation report, so from the actual duplicate sends to us noticing was overnight, worse than I'd like. Once I saw the mismatch I pulled the transmission logs and had the root cause — the retry job resending without checking Treasury's confirmation — narrowed down within about 40 minutes. I told my lead and the program manager as soon as I had the number of affected records, not after we'd fixed it. Recovery, meaning the reversing entries posted and verified against Treasury's file, took about three hours total. The postmortem's actual change was the confirmation check I mentioned, plus we added same-day reconciliation instead of next-morning, so now a mismatch like that would surface within a couple hours instead of overnight.
answers.says: Describes an incident in a system they operated, with a timeline and numbers (time from detection, time to recovery, number of affected cases). Explains, in their own words, what they looked at to triage the cause and the recovery decisions (including who they told and when), and can describe the postmortem's preventive measures and whether they actually worked afterward. If their own mistake caused it, they can describe, matter-of-factly, how they shared that without hiding it.

answers.text: Tell me about your experience and thinking on migrating from Java to Rust. If you have production Rust experience, tell me its scope; if not, tell me how you think you could realistically learn the differences from Java — ownership, lifetimes, async runtimes. Also tell me your thinking on how to decide a service boundary.
answers.answer: I'll be straight about this one — I haven't used Rust, not in production and not really on my own time either. What I know is secondhand: ownership catches memory issues at compile time instead of leaving them to a garbage collector, and that's supposed to make certain classes of bugs impossible rather than just less likely. I don't have a concrete plan for learning it yet, honestly. I'd want to sit down with the actual differences from Java — ownership, lifetimes, how async works without a thread-per-request model — before I'd feel comfortable saying how long that would take me. I'm willing to put the time in if it's part of the role, but I'd rather say that plainly than pretend I have a timeline I haven't actually worked out.
answers.says: If they have production Rust experience, they describe which part of production it was (e.g., why latency became an issue, how they cut the boundary with Java, the measurement results), with numbers and time frames, and can describe failures too. If they lack production experience, they explain the concrete differences from Java in ownership, lifetimes, and async runtimes in their own words, and describe a realistic learning plan (what they have already written, read, or been studying). In addition, they state a view that fits our approach — deciding a boundary and migrating while measuring, rather than a full rewrite — together with their own grounds for it.

answers.text: Have you ever, while responding to an urgent incident, felt tempted to skip review or the normal deployment procedure? Tell me what you actually did, and what you think would need to be in place to justify a decision to skip a step.
answers.answer: I try to avoid needing to skip anything, and mostly I've managed that, but there was one night during that duplicate-refund incident where I pushed the confirmation-check fix without our usual second reviewer, because it was 11pm and the alternative was letting more duplicate sends go out overnight while we found someone. Before I deployed it I posted in our team channel exactly what the change was and that I was shipping it without review given the situation, and I opened a real PR the next morning so someone actually looked at the diff after the fact. My rule for myself is: I only skip it when money is actively going out the door wrong in the meantime, and I say so before I act, not after. Outside that kind of situation I've never shipped without the normal review.
answers.says: Names a concrete experience of being forced to choose between the procedure and an emergency, and describes what they actually did. If they skipped it, they describe the steps — announcing it beforehand, recording it afterward, and following up with the normal procedure once recovered — together with the criteria for that skip decision. If they didn't skip it, they describe why (not shipping a change they can't verify, money is not a test environment) and an alternative way to move quickly and safely without cutting the procedure. Either way, their own judgment and its outcome come through as a concrete example.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you shared a mistake or a delay early, and about your experience with on-call, handling inquiries, or mentoring juniors. For both, please be concrete about what you yourself did.
answers.answer: A smaller one, but it's mine: I once pushed a config change that had a typo in a threshold value, which I noticed myself about twenty minutes later when a metric looked slightly off, before it had actually caused any real problem. I flagged it in the team channel right away rather than quietly fixing it and saying nothing, even though nobody had noticed yet. I've been on our on-call rotation for the refund system for about three years, one week in five, and it gets genuinely busy during filing season — I've had nights with six or seven pages. I've also spent time walking a newer engineer through how our reconciliation reports work and what to check first when the numbers don't match. I've never treated any of that as separate from the actual engineering work.
answers.says: Can describe a concrete example of sharing their own mistake or delay before it got worse — what, when, to whom, how it was communicated, and what happened as a result. Also names a real example of taking on on-call rotation, inquiry handling, or mentoring juniors as their own job (duration, frequency, approach), and can describe never having thought of it as ‘not my real job.’ Both are told as their own actions, including experience of sharing within a blameless culture.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you restored data consistency in a production Java service after an incident or a bug. What was broken, how did you pin down the scope, how did you fix it, and how did you confirm the fix worked?
answers.answer: A batch job that pulls refund amounts from the return-processing system stopped partway through one night after an upstream timeout, and it wasn't obvious at first — the job logs just showed it exited, not that it had left about 900 refund records in a half-computed state over roughly a two-hour window. I scoped it by querying for records with a null final-amount field but a non-null processing timestamp, which gave me the exact list. I fixed it by re-running the calculation for just those records and inserting fresh entries rather than updating the half-computed ones in place, then verified by comparing the recomputed totals against the source return-processing system for every record in that list before closing it out. My first guess was a smaller set, about 200 records — I'd only checked one table before realizing a second table had records in the same bad state.
answers.says: Names a concrete inconsistency in a production service they were responsible for (e.g., double counting, a missing journal entry, a batch job that stopped partway), and describes how they scoped the impact (query, count, time period), how they fixed it (a correcting record rather than an overwrite, a backfill), and how they verified the fix afterward (reconciliation, recalculation), with numbers. Can also describe it if their first read of the problem was wrong.

answers.text: If you were to move part of the ledger write path to Rust, where would you start, where would you place the boundary with Java, and what would you measure before and after the migration to make that call? If you've cut out a language or service boundary before, please answer in light of that experience.
answers.answer: I don't have hands-on experience carving out a language boundary, Rust or otherwise, so I want to be honest that this is more opinion than experience. My instinct is you'd want the boundary to be narrow and stateless if you can — something like a single write path with a clear interface — rather than anything that has to share a transaction with the rest of the system. I'd want to see latency and error rate measured before and after on whatever piece moves, and I'd want a period where both sides run and get compared before fully cutting over. But I haven't done that migration myself, so I can't tell you exactly where I'd draw that line on a real system.
answers.says: Can describe a general direction for migration, but it stays at generalities (‘measurement matters first,’ ‘migrate in stages’), without describing the concrete boundary location, the metrics to watch, or the decision criteria in their own words. Even when citing past experience carving out a boundary, they can't distinguish what they decided from ‘what the team did,’ and no numbers or failures come up.

answers.text: In Rust code you've actually written — production or a personal project, either is fine — tell me a spot where you got stuck on ownership, lifetimes, or async, and how you resolved it. If you haven't written any yet, just say so.
answers.answer: I haven't written any Rust code, production or personal project. I don't want to pad that out with something that sounds more impressive than it is — I've read about ownership and the borrow checker, but I haven't sat down and actually hit a compiler error myself, so I can't tell you a real story about getting stuck and working through it.
answers.says: Has never written Rust code and admits it, or substitutes talk of Java or unrelated career history for the question.

fit.says: Considering what it would be like for this person to work here, they can be judged as someone who would act in line with all of our working principles (argue with evidence, then follow the decision; do not hide; money is not a test environment; operations and support are equal work; decide the boundary before you rewrite). Throughout the candidate's account of their experience, they consistently show a stance of sharing incidents and mistakes without hiding them, treating on-call, support, and mentoring juniors as their own job, never skipping review and deployment procedures even in an emergency, and carrying out migrations based on measurement and agreement while respecting the team's decisions.
